profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for a methodology-oriented survey-plus-benchmark paper on catastrophic forgetting in incremental deep neural networks, intended for a continual learning workshop submission in six weeks and later expansion into a journal article. The team has already agreed on the broad theme—comparing exemplar-based, memory/regularization-based, and network-based approaches—but needs to plan the empirical companion section, decide what goes into the main comparison table, assign implementation and writing responsibilities, and set milestones. The expected outcome is a shared plan for which methods to cover first, how results will be assembled, what counts as a usable draft next week, and who owns the benchmark setup, literature matrix, and paper sections.

members.name: Dr. Leena Rao
members.expertise: Continual learning evaluation, benchmark design, and empirical ML methodology
members.background: Leads a small academic lab working on reliable evaluation of lifelong learning systems and has published survey-style and benchmarking papers in incremental learning.
members.private_state: She wants a credible workshop paper quickly without overcommitting compute, and is aiming for a broad methodology paper where the empirical section supports the argument rather than becoming a full-scale reproduction study.
hidden_assumptions: If a baseline already has released code or trustworthy published logs under a matching setup, using those numbers still counts as reproducing it for a methodology paper.
A 'main comparison table' can be considered ready for an internal draft once the structure is fixed and a few representative methods have stable numbers, even if many rows are still pending.

Methods are still comparable enough for the paper's main synthesis if they share the same dataset stream and rough memory regime, with protocol differences such as test-time task identity noted in footnotes rather than used as exclusion criteria.
The student/postdoc will interpret next week's milestone as an internal narrative checkpoint, not as a fully publication-grade artifact.

members.name: Aaron Kim
members.expertise: Deep learning implementation, experiment automation, and reproducibility pipelines for continual learning
members.background: Recently joined from an industry research group where benchmark claims were heavily scrutinized, and he typically builds unified training pipelines so every compared method is rerun under one codebase.
members.private_state: He wants the study to be robust enough to survive reviewer skepticism and hopes to turn the benchmark into a reusable artifact, so he is quietly optimizing for rigor and completeness over speed.
hidden_assumptions: To 'reproduce' a baseline, every method in the main table should be retrained end-to-end inside one common framework rather than relying on paper numbers or external checkpoints.
A 'main comparison table' is not really ready unless all selected methods are filled in with repeated runs and variability estimates, because partial tables invite misinterpretation.

Methods only belong in the main comparison if the inference protocol is genuinely identical, especially regarding single-head class-incremental testing versus settings that use task identity at test time.
When a milestone is stated casually in a planning meeting, it still refers to something polished enough to circulate to coauthors without major caveats.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to reproduce the baselines
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'reproduce the baselines under a common protocol.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means harmonizing the comparison at the reporting level: reuse released code, checkpoints, or published numbers when the setup already matches, and only rerun methods that are missing or clearly incompatible.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means rerunning every selected method from scratch in the same framework with the same training harness so the table is generated entirely in-house.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research, 'reproduce' is a prestige term that sounds precise but often spans anything from validating published numbers to full reimplementation, so both hear methodological rigor and do not feel a need to unpack the execution details.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include methods that have the 'same evaluation mechanism' or are in a 'comparable setting.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes this to mean methods run on the same sequential dataset family and similar memory-budget regime can appear together in the main synthesis, even if some use task identity at test time or slightly different classifier-head conventions, as long as those differences are annotated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes this to mean only methods that share the exact inference protocol—especially single-head class-incremental evaluation with no task labels at test time—should enter the main comparison table; anything else belongs outside the core benchmark.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely trying to avoid unfair apples-to-oranges comparisons, and the phrase 'same evaluation mechanism' feels sufficiently technical and settled that neither notices they are drawing the inclusion boundary at different levels of strictness.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the main table being ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'have the main comparison table ready by next Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'ready' means the table template is finalized, categories are fixed, and a few representative methods from each family have numbers so writing can proceed with placeholders for the remaining rows.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'ready' means the full selected method set is populated with stable results, ideally across multiple seeds and with memory/compute notes, because otherwise the table is not genuinely usable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Planning meetings often use milestone language as shorthand, and 'ready' feels like a shared managerial term even though researchers routinely apply very different completion standards depending on whether they are thinking about internal drafting or publication-quality evidence.
